title: Gateless Barrier, Case 41: Bodhidharma Pacifies the Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 41 of the Gateless Gate, "Bodhidharma Pacifies the Mind," in which the second ancestor Huike (Weike in the transcript) stands in the snow, cuts off his arm, and asks to have his mind put to rest. Nomon sets it beside Bodhidharma's exchange with Emperor Wu ("no merit," "vast emptiness, nothing holy," "I don't know") and the four disciples who answer with skin, flesh, bones, and marrow. A story of Nomon nearly mistaking a visiting Japanese teacher for the sangha's own teacher, until Norman Fischer set Nomon straight, shows how readily we look outside ourselves. Dogen's line on forgetting the self leads to the practice of "I don't know," and Nomon closes with July plans, including six practice leaders taking over the Wednesday talks.

sentences.text: *Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept.
I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's word.*
Good evening, everybody.
Well, we've reached a really famous and wonderful story in the Mumonkan, the Gateless Gate koan collection, Zen story collection.
Case 41 out of 48.
I'm so excited to be in the 40s.
It's a case about Bodhidharma.
As you might recall from long ago, there was another case about Bodhidharma that we'll also remind you about after we hear the main case here.
So here's the story.
*Bodhidharma faced the wall.
The second ancestor stood in the snow, cut off his arm and said, "Your disciple's mind has no peace as yet.
I beg you, master, please put it to rest."
Bodhidharma said, "Bring me your mind, and I will put it to rest."
The second ancestor said, "I have searched for my mind, but I cannot find it."
Bodhidharma replied, "I have completely put it to rest for you."*
So, setting aside for a moment the creepy amputation that they dropped in there, this is a wonderful famous story about our hamster wheel of a mind, right?
The way our mind drives us crazy.
And we want therefore to turn it into a thing that we can improve or fix, or maybe somebody else can fix it for us.
But we see through our practice and through our life that there's not exactly this thing called the mind that we can fix or pacify or improve.
And yet we seem to need to go through a process, right, through a journey, in order to realize that we can just let go of trying to fix ourselves.
And then we realize we actually are, in some fundamental way, okay just the way we are.
And that play seems often, maybe always, to need to involve other people.
There are many stories, of course, of meditation adepts going off on their own into the woods forever and stuff like that.
But the Zen tradition is so relational, so interactive.
And so this story implies multiple stories about interaction between the student and the teacher.
One of which they just referenced by talking about the second ancestor, who is a Chinese monk named Weike.
He's called the second ancestor because, in the end, in another famous Bodhidharma story, Bodhidharma is going to name this student as his successor.
It's a giveaway that says "the second ancestor."
The Chinese love ancestors and succession, and the Zen tradition received that from China.
Bodhidharma is the first ancestor and this is going to be a successor later, but in the beginning he is not, right?
That's not clear.
That's the other thing about these stories, that they seem so tidy: Zen stories, Greek mythology, all the stories.
They seem so tidy because we know how it works out.
But in real life, we don't know how it's going to work out.
It's helpful, I think, to remind ourselves of that: the character in the story doesn't know he's the second ancestor, even though that's what he is called in the story.
He just thinks he's like us, right?
A confused person trying to make some change, be a little calmer, be a little less crazy, find a way to navigate his life.
We don't really know much of anything about this particular person in terms of biography before he studied with Bodhidharma.
But we know he heard that there was this Indian meditation master living in a cave.
Like the hippies going to India in the 60s, and like so many other pilgrims over the eras, he wanted to know who this was.
One of the backstories here is that Bodhidharma is such an intense meditator, like nothing can really disturb him, and he doesn't get up for anything.
And Weka finds his cave, and it had some kind of door on it, I guess, and bangs on the door.
And Bodhidharma doesn't move.
He tells him to go away.
So Weka has to do something to convince Bodhidharma he's serious, and that's what the cutting off your arm thing is.
That flavor is retained in our Zen tradition for all these millennia too, right: that it's good to be able to do something to show that you're serious.

So in the Japanese monasteries, they have people wait in a special room by the gate for a few days or a week before they let them in, although it's usually a foregone conclusion that that's what's going to happen.
We don't exercise that very formally at Red Cedar Zen.
We don't make new people sit in front of the gate or sit in the Zoom waiting room or something like that.
That's what we should do, probably.
First time you come.
Yeah, so Kyler here got an easy, easy evening.
He should have just sat in the waiting room with nothing at all, just totally blank, and meditated.
Probably that's what we should do.
And [unclear: "if we look in the way"] and then we all look in the waiting room at the end of the evening, and if he's still there, that's like cutting off the arm.
We let him practice with us.
So that's part of the backstory: these students worked hard to show that they were really sincere.
One of several other famous stories about Bodhidharma is that when he first came to China from India, and here we should mention that we don't really know if he was a real person.
He's a myth.
There is apparently some archaeological and anthropological evidence that he probably existed, but none of it's very firm or convincing.
So it's a bit of a partisan thing, did Bodhidharma really exist.
Bodhidharma is not a Chinese name, did you catch that?
It's an Indian Dharma name, Bodhidharma, right, the light of Dharma, the awakening of Dharma.

So anyway, the other story is that when he first came to China, it happened to be in an era where the ruler of the southern kingdom of Liang... there were many eras in China with different constellations of kingdoms.
So only a few times was it all unified like it is now.
He arrived in the southern Chinese kingdom of Liang.
At that time, the emperor was already into Buddhism.
Buddhism had not been in China that long, and the emperor was creating Buddhist temples.
But the idea was there only had been a few monks from India and, I don't know, maybe those few monks didn't really remember everything.
So it was sort of like a rough approximation, a rough copy.
They didn't have much confidence in what they were doing at the time.
This was the fifth century.
Supposedly Bodhidharma arrives there in AD 520.
I don't know how they would have such a specific date for someone who we don't know if he exists, but they do.
And the emperor had been supporting this flourishing of this new religion, and maybe other temples as well.
And he heard there was a serious monk, so it was a big deal.
There only had been a few of them.
And it would be like us, I think, if a true Japanese Zen teacher showed up.
We would get all excited.
And in fact, that happened one time, about 20 years ago.
I can't remember the name of either character now, but an American Zen student came to Samish one time.
I can't remember his name.
He told us that he had a Japanese teacher and that that Japanese teacher was thinking about moving to this area.
And would we like to meet him?
I forget who was with me.
I don't know if you were there, Bob, or what.
Of course, I got all excited: oh, a real Japanese teacher.
Maybe he said he was enlightened, or implied it.
I don't know.
We were all younger.
We were so much younger then.
Then in the fall, a few months later, said Japanese teacher came to visit.
We were all excited, and we took him to the Dharma Hall.
He was rough and serious, which is kind of the style.
He asked if he could offer incense.
He had reasonable English.
I remember him offering incense.
It was the Dharma Hall and the Masonic Lodge upstairs, the previous one from the current one.
Very carefully offering incense and doing these very stiff, intense prostrations.
And then coming back up to me and [unclear: "big deep out of me"] and thanking me for letting him offer incense.
And then I think this guy, the American, had some property on [unclear: "Chuck in a drive"] that he was hoping to buy or something.
The whole thing was completely a pipe dream and none of it was actually going to happen.
But we got swept up in the story, because just like Emperor Wu in this story, we're like, oh, on some level, whoa, the real thing.
And this next part of the story is a little embarrassing.
I called up Norman a few days later and said, "Norman, Norman, wow, man, Japanese teacher coming in."
And this is one of the more polite things he ever said to me when I pissed him off, which was very few times.
He's not very piss offable, Norman.
He said, "Well, hmm, seems to me the sangha already has a teacher," being him.
I was like, "We think this Japanese guy is going to be our teacher."
He's like, "I think there already is a teacher."
And I snapped out of it, like you do.
Oh, oh, yeah.
Sorry.
Yeah.
How's the weather down there?
So anyway, we're so vulnerable to this, right?
We want to do it right, and we want to have the right teacher.
And if we find the right teacher, we'll do anything, right?

We'll drive them around and buy into an exciting fantasy about buying a multimillion dollar property and [unclear: "chucking out"] and having this new teacher, or cut off our arm or whatever we have to do.
So anyway, Emperor Wu, back in 520 AD.
Of course, he wants to see the visiting teacher.
And so he asked him about the flourishing.
Emperor Wu asked him about his efforts, and he says, "I have endowed temples and authorized ordination.
What is my merit?"
He's referring to the Buddhist concept of merit, a kind of cosmic positive energy that's generated through our activities.
The chanting we just did generates merit.
So Bodhidharma very famously gave this answer: no merit.
And so the emperor, of course, is taken aback.
He studied whatever was available in Buddhism, so he's shocked.
I think part of me was worried that exactly that was what the visiting Japanese teacher way back then was going to say.
I don't know if I thought it consciously, but he was really going to look around and say, "No merit.
I don't know what you guys are doing."
This is just not the thing.
But the emperor bounces back and asks Bodhidharma, "Well, what is the first principle of the holy teaching?"
If there's no merit, then how does it work?
And what's the principle?
And Bodhidharma said, "Vast emptiness, nothing holy."
So there is no holy teaching.
Vast emptiness, nothing holy.
Which is either threatening or liberating, right?
Depending on how you see all this, how you see your mind.
And then the third part of the exchange, this three-part story, is that the emperor asked him, "Well, who is sitting before me?"
Or some translations have, "Who is confronting me?"
And Bodhidharma said, "I don't know.
Who are you?
I don't know."
And then he heads off to his cave and many other legendary things happen.
So yeah, how do we understand our mind?
How are we seeking validation?
Do we require someone on the outside?
Is there an inside?
Is there an outside?
These funky stories just bring up so much.
Who are we, really?
And they also bring up how much we suffer when we have some fixed idea, right?
Some fixed idea of who we are, what the practice is, or what's supposed to happen.
And these last months under COVID have been pressing against that, right?
Pressing against all of our fixed ideas of who we are and what's supposed to be happening and what the world is like.
And if we cling to any of these ideas, we suffer.
But I think the thing that's easy to misunderstand is that it's not like there's a shortcut either.

It seems like we need to practice with our clinging and our suffering and our thinking we know who we are and what our mind is, and how do we fix it, and how do we get validation, and how do we do it right, and who is the true teacher.
And I am appreciating the part about my story of the visiting Japanese teacher and Norman, too: that sense of not noticing the treasures that are right in front of you.
And not noticing the treasures are right within you, which is always another part of the spiritual journey.
You feel such lack, right?
So you go on a great journey, only to discover, once you're exhausted and out of energy, once you can't look anymore, that you had it all along.
You had what you needed all along.
And a third, or maybe I'm on four now, I'm not sure, a famous teacher about Bodhidharma is at the end of his career.
So this is like the beginning of his career in China.
So we have beginning, middle, and end in the story.
It's a tidy story.
Which also gives out, which the scholars who argue that there was no Bodhidharma, that's one of their arguments, too: the story is a little too tidy.
And the ending of his career, before he vanishes again, he has four disciples.
And that's also humbling, a lifetime of effort, hardcore, famous first-end meditation teacher in China, four disciples over his whole time.
And so he brings the four disciples together and says, tell me what the true meaning of the teaching is.
What have you learned from me in all these years?
And whoever answers correctly will receive my Dharma, will become the next ancestor.
And so the four gather around.
And interestingly, a kind of cool thing, sorry, I realized I forgot to bring this up.
Of those four, one of them is actually a woman.
So that's kind of cool to notice that one of the earliest Zen stories has a nun in it, has a woman in it.
So it wasn't all men that were recorded.
*Bodhidharma asked the four disciples, can each of you say something to demonstrate your understanding?
The first named Daofu stepped forward and said, it, the Dharma, the way, is not bound by words and phrases, nor is it separate from words and phrases.
This is the function of the way.
And Bodhidharma said, you have attained my skin.
And then the nun Zongchur stepped up and said, it is like a glorious glimpse of the realm of Akshiyoba Buddha.
Never seen once, it need not be seen again.
Bodhidharma, you have attained my flesh.
And then another monk said, named Daoyu said, the four elements are empty.
The five skandhas are without actual existence.
Not a single Dharma can be grasped.
Bodhidharma said, you have attained my bones.
Finally, Weka, a character from story 41 here, Weka came forth, bowed deeply in silence and stood up straight.
Bodhidharma said, you have attained my marrow.*
So you win the prize.
But Dogen comments on this case in his essay on it.
He makes the point it's a mistake to think that one of these answers is better than another, and that it's a linear narrative, like it at first appears.
All of these expressions are completely an expression of the Dharma.
So let me just share the expressions, because oftentimes we study the story and skip over the first three, right?
Because you're like, okay, what's the real thing?
Just like Emperor Wu did, just like I did with the visiting Japanese teacher.
Like, what's the marrow?
But these are all deep, important teachings.
So the first one: this practice, this way, is not bound by words and phrases, nor is it separate from words and phrases.
This is the function of the way.
So we can't completely describe this, what we're trying to understand about our heart, about the mind, about the world, with words and phrases.
But it's not separate from words and phrases.
We also practice with language.
We practice with concepts.
So it's beyond concepts and it's not separate from concepts: we need both, right?
It's kind of a holding of both.
Conceptual and non-conceptual, we need both.
This is the function of the way, or the Tao, right?
And so the Tao is a sense of flow, conceptual and non-conceptual flowing together.
And then the second one, which is our nun, Zongzhi: it's like the glorious glimpse of the realm of Akshiyoba Buddha.
Once, sorry, seen once, it need not be seen again.
So I forgot to look up exactly the symbolism of Akshiyoba Buddha.
But we can say for now that it's a vision of awakening, of light, of clarity, of everything's okay.
And this is not far-out religious stuff exactly, even though it's framed that way.
We all have these moments, right?
Sometimes it seems to be framed in an aesthetic moment, seeing a sunset, or a relationship moment, a moment of loving connection.

And we think that it's about the sunset or about the person we love, but actually it's about this glimpse, this glorious glimpse into the realm of this bigger reality where everything is actually okay.
And you just need to see that once to penetrate, to really understand, and those glimpses are important and complete.
So that's good too, right?
Nothing wrong with that answer.
The third answer: the four elements are empty.
So emptiness means everything is not rigid and separate.
The word emptiness is confusing in English, although it's the same word that they use in Sanskrit for this concept.
But the four elements, being earth, air, water, earth, air, heat, fire, water, are empty.
So they're not really that separate.
They're interpenetrated and connected.
And the five skandhas are an early Buddhist formulation of the mental constructs that we mistake for ourselves.
The five skandhas are without actual existence.
And not a single Dharma can be grasped.
So you can't cling on to anything and think, oh, now I got that.
Now I have this, right?
It's all flowing and fluid and interpenetrated.
So that's a wonderful answer too.
And then the hero of the story from our frame as heroic thinkers, Weka, just bowed, just stood.
So that's also very beautiful, right?
We talk too much.
And that's another thing that's kind of beautiful, in a way, about the COVID time, right?
We're all being a little quieter, in some ways.
We're on a lot of Zoom calls, some of us.
But the basic mode of reality, the basic mode of society, is more upright, more silent, right?
So that's a blessing too.
It's the marrow.

So some stories about Bodhidharma to inspire us to just keep on the journey, keep exploring, keep wondering, being committed, noticing when we get caught by this deep desire to be validated by something or someone, or this deep delusion that we are somehow just our ideas about who we are: just our thoughts, just our thinking, just our personality, just our self.
And go look.
If you try to find that self, there's nothing to find.
Dogen's later teaching is a beautiful echo of that, isn't it, in Genjokoan?
*To practice the way is to study.
To study the way is to study the self.
And to study the self is to forget the self.*
So case 41 is a forgetting-the-self teaching.
"Bring me your mind and I will heal it for you.
I will pacify it for you."
"I've searched.
I've searched and searched and searched for a mind."
Who am I?
The more I think about it, the more I don't know, right?
Just like Bodhidharma's answer to Emperor Wu.
"Who are you?"
"I don't know."
There are lots of kinds of "I don't know," right?
This is a certain kind of "I don't know," deep in our gut.
It's an "I don't know" that's a result of practice over years, not just "oh, fuck it, I don't know," but like, *I don't know*.
The changing of the times has that quality too, right?
We keep thinking we know what's going to happen to each of us in different ways, and we're reading media, or some of us are actually doing deeper background reading.
Maybe some of us here actually downloaded scientific papers.
That would be wonderful, when you figure out what's going to happen with the virus.
And that's useful, right?
So this way is like the first students said: not separate from words and phrases.
So it's not separate from science.
It's not separate from predictions and not separate from information.
We need all that.
But it's not bound by that, right?
It's not knowable.
Nobody knows.
Literally nobody knows what's going to happen.
We have predictions based on the past and based on science, right?
About vaccines and immunity and antibodies and so on and so forth.
But we really don't know.
And in the meantime, we don't know what's going to happen to human systems after they go through whatever it is they're going to go through or keep going through.
We don't know.
Our cities and towns and culture may look very different in a couple of years.
Really might.
We don't know.

We also have a lot of faith that, in addition to running around and trying to figure it out, it's a great blessing for us and for the world to sit and watch, sit and face the wall, have part of our life be devoted not to running around and figuring it all out, but to stopping.
They say that Bodhidharma faced the wall.
So we have the tradition of a seven day retreat, that's the official length of sesshin.
They say Bodhidharma faced the wall for seven years without moving once.
We don't worry about digestion or stuff like that in these stories.
And just to make sure we do thorough Bodhidharma, other famous myths about him were that he started nodding off, a few years in, maybe.
So he ripped his eyelids off and threw them on the ground.
And when they landed on the ground, the first tea plants sprouted.
So from then on, Zen students have drunk strong green tea.
Although we're New World Zen students, so we drink coffee.
Which reminds me of a couple years ago, I got to do a more intense koan-based, sort of pure, if that's the right word, Zen training at a temple in Honolulu.

So here's a little about Bodhidharma in case 41.
Bodhidharma pacifies the mind.
I hope you're finding these stories helpful.
Oh, one last thing about Bodhidharma actually.
A famous four-line teaching is attributed to Bodhidharma.
Since we're translating from Chinese, we don't get the full effect.
But in Chinese, each line is the same number of characters.
So it's kind of like this powerful little brick of text.
Most Chinese poems and Chinese verses have the same number of characters, one after the next.
So this was probably written later.
But these are the so-called four principles of Bodhidharma, which are also the four principles of Zen.
And they are:
*Zen is a special transmission outside the sutras, with no dependence on words or phrases, directly pointing to the human mind, seeing into one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.
A special transmission outside the sutras,*
*with no dependence on words or phrases, directly pointing to the human mind, seeing into one's nature and attaining Buddhahood.* So that's our MO: just direct.
We are the A train of Buddhism.
But it's also not completely true, because that was not written by Bodhidharma.
That's very clear from scholarly work.
It was written a couple hundred years later, maybe 300 years later.
And it was written by Tang dynasty monks who were all highly educated in the Chinese system and wrote tons and tons and tons of books about how there's no words and letters.
But that's great too, right?
It's both, right?
It's both.
And it's exactly the same as with Bodhidharma's first student in his exit interview with them.
It both depends on words and phrases and does not depend on words and phrases and is not separate from words and phrases.
